source.title: On the origin of neural scaling laws: from random graphs to natural language
source.authors: Maissam Barkeshli; Alberto Alfarano; Andrey Gromov

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some equations and figure content are flattened or imperfectly rendered, but the paper is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling curves and compute-optimal allocations, and critically examines how fitting method, parameter counting, parameterization, and fit window affect the resulting exponents and conclusions.
record.gate_note: The study reports fitted loss exponents, fit-error comparisons, and compute-optimal exponents for its experiments and reanalyses. Results merely cited from other work are not recorded. Values used only to choose learning rates or other hyperparameters are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own loss-scaling and compute-optimal curves for small transformers on natural language (Fineweb-edu) and synthetic sequence data. It also reanalyses Pythia and raw Chinchilla data. It argues that exponents and the compute-optimal split depend on the irreducible-loss offset, the fitting method, parameter counting, parameterization and the fit window. That bears directly on V1, V3, V5 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Additions: the authors report that a 2-layer, context-100 transformer reproduces the Chinchilla split when embeddings are counted and the Kaplan split when they are not. They give preliminary evidence that µP is more parameter-efficient. They argue that scaling laws arise even without power-law structure in the data, and that αD falls monotonically as data complexity rises.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than reproducing the original large-model scaling experiments, the paper trains small transformers on graph walks and language data and reanalyzes published Pythia and Chinchilla results using alternative fitting procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted exponents depend on including the irreducible-loss offset and on the fitting window. Compute-optimal exponents differ when embedding parameters are included or excluded and between standard parameterization and µP.

fits_no_version.finding: Neural scaling laws appear for next-token prediction on unbiased random walks on Erdős–Rényi graphs, whose data have no power-law structure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law loss scaling does not require power-law structure in the training data.

record.problems: The study itself notes that compute-optimal curves are derived from fitted surfaces and are clipped near sampled-grid boundaries; Chinchilla data have too few fixed-D points for a parameter-scaling fit; fit parameters are sensitive to the chosen window; and µP efficiency results are preliminary and not established at larger scales. Several synthetic-data results require careful hyperparameter grid searches.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many separate fitted curves for individual fixed-token or fixed-parameter settings in Figures 1, 4–8, 11–14, 20–23. These were not all included as separate rows because the captions also provide aggregate exponents by dataset and setup; the row set prioritizes those reported aggregates, fit-method comparisons, compute-optimal exponents, and explicit setup sensitivities.

untested.parts: No fit on small runs is tested against much larger runs.
2- vs 4-layer models are compared, but not at a fixed parameter count. There is no width/depth sweep at fixed N.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer settings. Only synthetic sequence data (graph walks, bigrams, transformer-generated text) is tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
Only small transformers (2–4 layers, up to about 1B parameters) are tested on Fineweb-edu. Reanalysis of Pythia and Chinchilla covers larger models but spans limited ranges.

missing.what: 4-layer SP transformer on Fineweb-edu: αD=0.391 (sd 0.060), βN=0.550 (sd 0.020); compute-optimal a=0.527, b=0.470

ER graph with 50K nodes and 2M edges: κ=0 gives α=2.443, β=1.361, a=0.174, b=0.826; κ=1 gives α=2.169, β=0.847, a=0.205, b=0.788. The L(N)D power law is only about 3x better than the exponential fit for κ=0.
Compute-optimal exponents on synthetic data, showing the split depends on the data: bigram a=0.366/b=0.632; ER 8K a=0.264/b=0.738; T1L 0.417/0.580; T2L 0.400/0.591
On the µP language experiments, the 2d Chinchilla fit has about 30–40x worse MSE than NN or kernel regression

record.verdict_notes: All rows that link to V1 use natural language. Graph-walk and synthetic-sequence rows are moved to V5 as a non-text training regime; this is a judgment call, since V5's examples are images, video and repeated or fine-tuning data. µP and SP language runs differ in context length and batch size, confounding the µP comparison. The Chinchilla reanalysis uses data from an original source, but this study is not itself an original, so verdicts are allowed. r24 shows that fitting method barely changes the compute-optimal split, which partly runs against V7 on the method axis.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests parameter- and token-dependent loss fits on selected language and synthetic datasets, not a comprehensive range of production-scale language models or training setups.
It compares fit quality in observed data, but does not fit on small runs and then test predictions against runs orders of magnitude larger.

The compute-optimal curves are assessed in selected datasets and model setups; the study does not establish a universal allocation rule across all model families, training schedules, or compute ranges.
Although two- and four-layer models are reported, the study does not isolate depth or width at a fixed parameter count to test whether architecture details change loss only slightly.
No image or video modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The paper demonstrates sensitivity to some fitting and setup choices, but does not provide a comprehensive sensitivity analysis across optimization algorithms and datasets.
